references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew: After Jesus had finished all these words (ἐπλήρωσεν/ἐτέλεσεν), he went on. Both verses mark the transition from Jesus' speech (the Sermon on the Mount/Sermon on the Plain) to the next narrative.
Matthew's parallel account of the centurion's servant in Capernaum. Jesus enters Capernaum and meets a centurion who asks for help—the same event that follows in Luke 7:2ff.
Jesus goes down to Capernaum, which is a recurring theme in the Gospel of Luke. Capernaum served as a base for Jesus' ministry in Galilee.
Jesus' speech on the plain (the Sermon on the Plain) preceding Luke 7:1. The verse marks the conclusion of this speech: 'When he had finished all his words to the people who were listening.'

A similar transitional formula in Matthew: 'When Jesus had finished giving these instructions to his twelve disciples...'—the same literary pattern where Jesus finishes a speech and then moves on to the next place.

Moses finished writing the words of the law in a book. The expression about finishing (ἐπλήρωσεν) all the words has its background in Old Testament tradition, where important speeches and words are formally concluded, just as Moses concluded his words to the people.
Moses finished speaking all these words to all Israel. Luke uses a similar formulation that points to Jesus as the new Moses who finishes his speech to the people (λαός).
